body:
You are drafting text for "Curse of Strahd", a single-player CRPG built on the D&D 5e Curse of Strahd campaign. Reply with ONLY the slot lines in the format at the end (no preamble, no commentary, no code fence).

## Who the Narrator is
An old gothic storyteller who has watched a great many adventurers walk into Barovia and very few walk out. Not the party's enemy and not its friend. Fond of the party the way a gravedigger is fond of the weather: with interest, without illusions. Never gloats over a failure, never cheers a success. Notices.

## Rules
1. Second person, present tense. "You step inside." Never "the party steps inside", never past tense. Never use character names (the lord of the castle is "the count" or "the master of the house", never his name).
2. One or two sentences per line. The second sentence is usually the turn: the irony, the dread, the joke.
3. Ominous, dryly funny, never cruel. Laugh at the house, the dark, the situation. Never at the player.
4. No facts the party hasn't earned. Describe only what the characters can perceive.
5. No modern slang, no winks at the player, no game terms (no "HP", "roll", "level", "action", "spell slot", "save", "check", "DC", "damage").
6. Concrete senses over adjectives: a smell, a sound, a temperature.
7. Plain punctuation: commas, colons, full stops. No em-dashes, no semicolons, no ellipses.
8. Each Narrator line is at most 35 words. Most are 18 to 28. Option labels (marked OPTION) are at most 10 words, written as what the party does ("Wait for the fire to burn low.").
9. Respect the dead: be wry about a corpse's circumstances, never about the corpse.

## The place
Castle Ravenloft is the home of the vampire lord of Barovia. These slots are about a hidden way far below the castle's dungeon, which we are adding, in our own words. All of it is ours, not copied from any book, so invent small concrete details freely, but keep to the facts below.

- THE LOW DOOR: in the south wall of the dungeon hall, behind a cold iron brazier, stands a low iron door that is easy to miss. Behind it a narrow stair winds down into the dark.
- THE WESTERN STAIR: a long stair of worn steps going down, turning at a broad landing. In the landing floor a warding glyph is cut into the stone: a circle of pale lines. Whoever steps on it raises an image of the count, tall, pale, in black with a red lining, who comes at the intruders. The image is made of wax: the first blow that lands melts it into a puddle of wax and a smell of candle-ends. Past the landing the stair goes on down to the brazier room.
- THE BRAZIER ROOM: a square vaulted chamber with a high ceiling. In its middle stands a broad stone brazier burning with a tall white flame that gives no heat at all. Around the brazier's rim are seven cup-shaped hollows, each holding a smooth coloured stone: violet, orange, red, green, indigo, blue and yellow. Above the brazier an hourglass hangs in the air by nothing, all its sand in the top bulb, and a verse is cut round its base. Throwing one of the stones into the flame turns the flame that stone's colour and makes the sand begin to fall, and then anyone who steps into the fire is carried away in a blink to another place far off. In two deep alcoves stand two iron knights, huge, visors down. They are really golems and they move only if someone attacks the brazier, the hourglass or one of them.
- WHERE EACH STONE LEADS (the verse must hint, never name outright):
  violet: the white guard tower high in the snow of the mountain pass.
  orange: the open roofs and peak of this same castle, under the sky.
  red: a tall house of lore and learning, the tower of an old monster hunter.
  green: where the coffins are kept, the castle's catacombs.
  indigo: the rooms where the count's brides sleep.
  blue: the ancient temple of amber buried in the mountain, where old magic was born.
  yellow: the count's own tomb.
- THE CENTRE STAIR: a second flight down from the south side of the brazier room, ending in a low black passage with fog creeping up it.
- THE TUNNEL: a long low tunnel cut through the black rock the castle stands on. Fog drifts along the floor, the ceiling barely clears a tall person's head, the floor is wet and slick, and the stonework is newer than the castle above it. Somewhere along it a hidden trapdoor of polished stone tips whoever steps on it into a chute. The tunnel ends at a low arch into the castle's catacombs.
- THE CHUTE: a steep chute of black polished marble, slick as ice, with no handholds. It drops the unwary into a prison cell under the dungeon hall, and it cannot be climbed back up without magic.

## What to write
Write one line for each slot below. A slot with a letter suffix (a, b) is a variant or a separate outcome of the same moment. Some slots are the Narrator's lines (second person, as above). Slots marked OPTION are the words on a menu button, not narration.

The low door and the stair:
D01  Narrator, entering the little nook behind the low iron door in the dungeon hall: a narrow stair winding down, cold air rising, the door shut behind you or open at your back.
W01  Narrator, entering the western stair: long worn steps going down, your footsteps coming back at you a beat late.
W02  Narrator, the party finds the glyph in the landing floor (a careful search succeeds): pale lines cut into the stone, a circle that has been waiting.
W03  Narrator, someone steps on the glyph: it flares and the count steps out of the light, tall, pale, in black with a red lining. Frightening, a half-second of dread.
W04  Text shown when the fight with the wax image begins: the image advances with one gloved hand raised.
W05  Narrator, the first blow lands and the image melts: it slumps into a puddle of wax and a smell of candle-ends. Dry, relieved.

The brazier room:
R01  Narrator, entering the brazier room: the vault, the tall white flame that gives no warmth, the hourglass hanging in the air, the two iron knights in their alcoves.
R02  Narrator, examining the brazier: seven coloured stones lying in cups round the rim, the flame white and cold.
R03  Narrator, examining the hourglass: it hangs in the air by nothing, the sand all in the top, a verse cut round its base. Lead in to the verse.
R04a Narrator, examining the iron knights: two figures of black iron in deep alcoves, visors down, waiting.
R04b Narrator, examining the iron knights after they have been broken: iron rubble and two empty alcoves.
R05  Narrator, examining the brazier after the knights were broken: the flame white and cold as ever, the stones still lying in their cups, no one left to mind them.

The verse on the hourglass (seven separate lines for seven stones; each one begins with the colour and hints at the place, as a riddle, without naming it; 12 to 24 words each; a little rhyme is welcome but not required):
V01  violet
V02  orange
V03  red
V04  green
V05  indigo
V06  blue
V07  yellow

Throwing the stones (one short line for each, the flame changing to that colour and the sand starting to fall; 10 to 18 words):
T01  violet
T02  orange
T03  red
T04  green
T05  indigo
T06  blue
T07  yellow
T08  Narrator, stepping into the coloured fire: no heat, no pain, a rush like falling upward, then somewhere else. One or two sentences.
T09  Narrator, none of the stones means anything to you yet (when the party has not been to any of the places the verse hints at, the stones are only coloured pebbles).

The brazier menu (OPTION labels, at most 10 words):
O01  OPTION: throw the violet stone into the fire.
O02  OPTION: throw the orange stone into the fire.
O03  OPTION: throw the red stone into the fire.
O04  OPTION: throw the green stone into the fire.
O05  OPTION: throw the indigo stone into the fire.
O06  OPTION: throw the blue stone into the fire.
O07  OPTION: throw the yellow stone into the fire.
O08  OPTION: step into the coloured fire.
O09  OPTION: let the fire go back to white and step away.
O10  OPTION: read the verse on the hourglass.
O11  OPTION: strike one of the iron knights.
O12  OPTION: smash the hourglass.
O13  OPTION: kick the brazier over.
O14  OPTION: leave the brazier alone.

Waking the knights (Narrator, the moment the fight begins; one or two sentences each):
G01  someone strikes an iron knight: the blow rings like a bell and both visors lift.
G02  someone smashes the hourglass: it shatters, sand pours out, and the knights step forward out of their alcoves.
G03  someone kicks the brazier over: coals that give no heat scatter, and iron groans in the alcoves.
G04  Text shown when the fight begins (generic): two iron knights come out of the alcoves, shaking dust from their joints.

The way on, and the fall:
C01  Narrator, entering the centre stair: a long flight down into a low black passage, fog creeping up the steps like a tide.
T10  Narrator, entering the tunnel: the low roof, the wet slick floor, the fog at ankle height, the stonework too new for the castle above.
T11  Narrator, the party finds the trapdoor in the tunnel floor (a careful search succeeds): a seam of polished stone, the fog draining into it.
T12  Narrator, someone steps on the trapdoor and it tips: a hair of warning, then the floor is gone.
F01  Narrator, the fall down the marble chute: black polished stone, no handholds, a long fast slide in the dark, then a cold cell floor. Two sentences.
F02  Narrator, examining the mouth of the chute high in the wall of the cell: polished black marble, wet, no handholds, no way up without magic.
F03  OPTION: climb up the chute with Spider Climb.
F04  OPTION: float up the chute with Levitate.
F05  OPTION: fly up the chute.
F06  OPTION: leave the chute alone.
F07  Narrator, climbing, floating or flying back up the chute to the tunnel: the long dark slide in reverse.

## Output format (exactly)
One slot per line, the slot id, a colon, a space, then the text. No blank lines needed. Example:
X01: Example text goes here, one or two sentences.
X02: Example option label.


Finish without sending messages to anyone else.
result:
D01: A narrow stair winds down into the dark behind the low iron door, breathing cold air into your face. Whatever waits below has been kept off the household maps.
W01: Long, worn steps lead you down into the dark. Your own footsteps come back to you a beat late, as if the stair is counting.
W02: Pale lines are cut into the stone of the landing floor, forming a neat circle in the dust. It has been waiting a long time for a boot.
W03: The pale circle flares, and the count steps out of the sudden light in black silk lined with red. For half a heartbeat, your blood forgets how to move.
W04: The pale figure of the count comes at you in silence, one gloved hand raised to strike.
W05: Your blow lands and the master of the house slumps into a warm puddle of tallow and a smell of candle-ends. Even his jokes have a way of lingering.
R01: A high vaulted room opens around a stone brazier burning with a tall white flame that gives no warmth. Above it an hourglass hangs upon nothing, while two huge iron knights wait in deep alcoves.
R02: Seven smooth stones of different colours rest in cup-shaped hollows round the brazier rim. Between them, the tall white fire burns as cold as well water.
R03: The hourglass hangs in the empty air with all its pale sand gathered in the upper bulb. Around its base, a quiet hand has cut a verse into the stone.
R04a: Two huge figures of black iron stand in deep alcoves with their visors down. They do not breathe, which saves them a great deal of trouble down here.
R04b: Broken plates and twisted joints of black iron litter the floor before two empty alcoves. The room is no warmer for their passing, only quieter.
R05: The white flame still burns without heat and the seven coloured stones still wait in their cups. There is no one left in the alcoves to mind what you touch.
V01: Violet casts you high where the white watchtower freezes in the mountain pass, keeping its cold vigil above the snow.
V02: Orange lifts you to the wet slate and high peaks of this very house, under a sky that never clears.
V03: Red sends you to a tall house of old books and older scars, where a hunter of monsters keeps his watch.
V04: Green drops you one floor deeper into the quiet dark, where the cold stone boxes of this house are kept in rows.
V05: Indigo brings you to the perfumed dark of the lower beds, where the master's brides lie in their long, unbreathing sleep.
V06: Blue carries you into the mountain's heart and its house of ancient amber, where old dark powers first learned to speak.
V07: Yellow lays you down in the deepest vault of all, beside the master's own cold bed of earth and stone.
T01: The violet stone drops in, the cold flame turns purple, and the first grains of sand begin to fall.
T02: You cast the orange stone in, the fire flares like autumn leaves, and the hanging sand begins to run.
T03: The red stone sinks into the brazier, turning the cold flame blood-bright as the sand starts to slip down.
T04: You toss the green stone into the fire, waking a pale sickly glow as the sand begins its fall.
T05: The indigo stone vanishes into the flame, dyeing it the colour of a bruise while the sand starts to trickle.
T06: You drop the blue stone in, the tall flame turns the colour of winter ice, and the sand begins to pour.
T07: The yellow stone strikes the brazier, turning the cold fire to pale gold as the sand starts to run.
T08: You step into the coloured flame and feel no heat at all, only a sudden rush like falling upward through cold water. Then the stone floor of the brazier room is gone.
T09: The seven stones gleam in their hollows like bright pebbles from a riverbed. Without knowing the places in the verse, one colour is as blind a leap as another.
O01: Throw the violet stone into the fire.
O02: Throw the orange stone into the fire.
O03: Throw the red stone into the fire.
O04: Throw the green stone into the fire.
O05: Throw the indigo stone into the fire.
O06: Throw the blue stone into the fire.
O07: Throw the yellow stone into the fire.
O08: Step into the coloured fire.
O09: Let the fire turn white again and step back.
O10: Read the verse cut around the hourglass.
O11: Strike one of the iron knights.
O12: Smash the hanging hourglass.
O13: Kick the stone brazier over.
O14: Leave the brazier alone.
G01: Your blow rings against the black iron like a church bell. In both alcoves, heavy visors lift over empty dark.
G02: Glass shatters in mid-air and pale sand spills across the flagstones. In the alcoves, two pairs of iron boots take their first step forward.
G03: Cold coals scatter across the stone floor without a single spark of heat. Deep in the alcoves, heavy iron joints groan awake.
G04: Two huge iron knights step out of their alcoves, shaking centuries of grey dust from their joints.
C01: A second flight of stone steps leads down from the south wall into a low black passage. Pale fog creeps up the stairs to meet your boots like a slow tide.
T10: The black rock ceiling barely clears your head, and ankle-deep fog drifts over the wet, slick floor. The chisel marks in the stone are fresh enough to make a careful mason wonder.
T11: Ahead of you, the creeping fog drains away into a neat square seam of polished stone. Someone has gone to great trouble to make the floor look solid.
T12: A faint click under your boot is all the warning the mason left you. Then the polished stone tips, and the floor is gone.
F01: Polished black marble takes your feet out from under you in a long, fast slide through the dark with nothing to catch your hands. You meet the cold stone floor of a cell at the bottom.
F02: High up in the cell wall, the mouth of the black marble chute gleams wet and slick as river ice. No fingers made of flesh and bone will ever find a hold in it.
F03: Walk up the slick chute like a spider.
F04: Float up the dark chute on borrowed air.
F05: Fly back up the black marble chute.
F06: Leave the chute alone.
F07: You rise back up the narrow black throat of polished marble, watching the wet stone slide past in reverse. The tunnel waits above with its trapdoor still yawning open.
